competitors.name: Free printable PDF/Word/Sheets templates (TypeCalendar, 101Planners, opendocs, Printabulls, Carepatron, template.net)
competitors.model: free, ad-supported SEO content farms; some upsell a paid editor
competitors.note: THE REAL COMPETITOR. Dominates every search for 'medication schedule chart'. Wins on zero friction and instant print. Loses badly on: fixed tiny type you cannot enlarge, generic grids you must hand-fill in ballpoint, no way to revise next month without rewriting the whole thing, and cluttered ad-choked pages. 101Planners is the closest to us, an in-browser log maker that explicitly says nothing is sent anywhere.

competitors.name: KeptWell Medication Schedule Builder
competitors.model: free tool, no account; company sells paid account-based plans (record organizing, family sharing)
competitors.note: Closest direct analogue and the one to study. Inputs patient name, med/dose/frequency, optional purpose/prescriber/refill date; outputs a PDF with a Morning/Noon/Evening/Bedtime grid at 8am/12/6pm/9pm plus a summary list; can emit a blank grid. Weaknesses we can exploit: it round-trips through a server ('we build the schedule and send it back to your browser'), the times are fixed defaults you 'adjust by hand', and there is no large-print mode, no allergy/emergency block, and no local save for re-editing.

competitors.name: Medisafe
competitors.model: was freemium, now effectively paid, free tier capped at 2 medications (Oct 2024), full paywall Jan 1 2026 after a 14-day trial; ~$4.99/mo, annual quoted variously at $39.99 and $59.88
competitors.note: Category leader by installs and the default recommendation in every 'best of' roundup. Deep features: drug-interaction checks, Medfriend caregiver alerts, dose logging. Utterly wrong shape for our job, it is a phone reminder for the patient, not a document for the fridge; printing/reporting is premium. Its 2026 paywall just orphaned millions of users and is the single biggest opening in this category right now.

competitors.name: MyTherapy
competitors.model: genuinely free, no ads, account optional-ish
competitors.note: The strongest free rival and the app most roundups now push Medisafe refugees toward. Clean UI, symptom journal, monthly health report you can print for a doctor. Still a reminder app: the printed output is a clinical report, not a legible-at-three-feet fridge card, and the whole model assumes a smartphone in the patient's hand.

competitors.name: Vial of Life / File of Life
competitors.model: free paper kits, distributed by fire departments, EMS, county aging services and senior centers
competitors.note: Not an app, the incumbent CONVENTION, and the reason our artifact belongs on a fridge at all. A medical-info form in a baggie or magnetic pocket on the refrigerator, with a red decal on the front door/window so paramedics know to look. EMS is trained to check the fridge. Weakness: hand-written on a photocopied form, illegible, chronically out of date. Enormous free win if our card prints Vial-of-Life-compatible.

competitors.name: Etsy / Gumroad paid printable medication trackers
competitors.model: paid one-time PDF, roughly $3-$8 (mchpharmacists, havenandhalo, presslyco and dozens more)
competitors.note: A live cottage industry, pharmacist-branded monthly med charts, 12-month refill calendars, caregiver daily-care binders. Proves people will pay for a nicer-looking version of a free thing. All static PDFs: no typing, no editing, no reflow when the med list changes.

competitors.name: Google Docs / Excel / a handwritten index card
competitors.note: What most families actually do, and the honest baseline. Infinitely flexible, zero learning curve, already on the machine. Loses on layout labor, nobody wants to fight table cells at 11pm on discharge day, and on the fact that the DIY version is almost never large-print or one page.

competitors.name: Hero / pill-dispenser hardware + companion apps, and pharmacy portals (Drugs.com My Med List, mediteo)
competitors.note: Hero's 'Download Medication Report' and mediteo's PDF export are the only mainstream print paths, and both sit behind a device purchase or an account. Drugs.com's My Med List needs a login. All of them treat the printout as an afterthought export, never as the product.

complaints.complaint: Medisafe killed the free tier, capped at 2 meds in Oct 2024, then a hard paywall on Jan 1 2026 after a 14-day trial. Users called charging vulnerable people an annual fee 'price gouging'. The bite: the average person with a chronic condition takes 4 to 5 daily meds, so the free tier is useless to precisely the people who need it.
complaints.source: pillo.care 'Medisafe Is Not Free Anymore' and 'Is Medisafe Still Free in 2026'; wellnestapp.app Medisafe subscription alternative guide; summarized Trustpilot/App Store review sentiment
complaints.weWinIf: Unlimited medications, forever, with no counter, no 'upgrade to add another', no trial clock. Say it out loud on the landing page: 'Add as many medications as you actually take.' A visible med count with no cap next to it is a quiet flex.

complaints.complaint: You cannot view, export, or transfer your own medication history without paying first. Cloud-first health apps make access to your own data conditional, and the terms changed underneath people who had years of records in there.
complaints.weWinIf: The data never leaves the device, and export is free and one tap: printable card, PDF, and a plain JSON/CSV file. Add an explicit 'Export everything' button that works before you have paid anything, because there is nothing to pay.

complaints.complaint: CareZone, for years a top-recommended med app, later Walmart Wellness, was retired Jan 31 2023 and accounts that were not migrated were deactivated. People who had built their parent's whole med history in it lost it.
complaints.source: Caring Village 2026 medication reminder app review noting the retirement; Walmart Wellness shutdown notice
complaints.weWinIf: Make the printed card the deliverable, not the account. Frame it: 'The card works if we disappear.' Back it with local-file export and a permanent, versioned static build. This is our single strongest emotional argument and it should be one sentence on the homepage.

complaints.complaint: Unskippable full-screen video ads that fire immediately AFTER you log a dose, 30+ seconds you cannot close, repeated for every med in a multi-dose regimen.
complaints.source: Google Play reviews of free pill reminder apps, aggregated in pillo.care 'Best Free Medication Reminder App for Android (2026)'
complaints.weWinIf: Zero ads, zero interstitials, zero third-party scripts, and prove it, not just claim it. A 'no network requests' line in the privacy page plus a CSP that literally cannot phone home. Consider showing the tip jar only after the card has printed, never before.

complaints.complaint: 'My Meds had teeny tiny icons that were not suitable for the eyes of an older adult, and might even confuse someone in their 30s.' Older-adult test panel rejected 17 of the apps they tried for crashes, confusing interfaces, bad databases, or missing export.
complaints.source: TechEnhancedLife citizen-research panel, 'Best Pill Reminder App: Explorer Choice'
complaints.weWinIf: Ship a real type-size control (not a browser-zoom shrug) with 18 / 22 / 28pt output presets, and make the DEFAULT already large. Minimum 44 to 48px tap targets in the editor. No icon-only controls anywhere, every control has a word on it.

complaints.complaint: 'Seniors are defeated by complicated menus, confusing icons, and apps that require six taps just to schedule a pill reminder.'
complaints.source: yougot.ai, 'Best Reminder Apps for Seniors: Beyond Large Buttons'
complaints.weWinIf: One screen, one scroll, no menus, no modals, no onboarding wizard. Adding a medication is: type name, tap a time-of-day chip, done. Target four taps from cold open to a printable card with one med on it.

complaints.complaint: Medication databases return garbage: 'we searched for amlodipine five different times and each time Med Coach returned different results.' Autocomplete that fights you is worse than no autocomplete.
complaints.weWinIf: Do not ship a half-broken drug database (we cannot anyway, no backend). Ship a plain, fast, forgiving text field that never rewrites what the user typed, plus a small bundled offline list of the ~300 most common generics purely as optional spelling help. Never auto-correct, only suggest.

complaints.complaint: Reminders fire at the wrong time, Care4Today alerted 30 minutes early, 'not good if your medication has to be taken on a precise schedule.' Other apps just froze (Pill Reminder by RV App Studio).
complaints.weWinIf: Sidestep it entirely and say so: this is not a reminder app, it has no notifications to get wrong. Position that as a feature, 'nothing to fail at 8am.' Then be reliable at the one thing we do: the card must render identically every time and print without clipping.

complaints.complaint: The free printable templates are dead grids, you download a PDF, then hand-write into 1/4-inch boxes in ballpoint. Sites that DO let you fill them in (DocHub, pdfFiller) push you into sign-up or a paywall to download the completed file.
complaints.source: DocHub and pdfFiller medication-list template listings; the template roundups at typecalendar.com, opendocs.com, 101planners.com
complaints.weWinIf: Typed, not handwritten, real text at real size, laid out automatically. And the download is unconditional: no email wall, no watermark, no 'create a free account to save'. This is the exact gap between us and the #1 Google result for our category.

complaints.complaint: Brand-vs-generic name confusion causes double dosing, a family gives both 'Norvasc' and 'amlodipine' not knowing they are the same drug. Roughly 25% of reported medication errors come from look-alike/sound-alike name confusion; safety guidance explicitly says put BOTH names and the indication on the label.
complaints.source: PBA Health '9 Tips for Avoiding Confusion Between Drugs'; Pennsylvania Patient Safety Advisory on drug name confusion; FDA drug-name-confusion consumer guidance
complaints.weWinIf: Two name fields on every row, brand and generic, both printed, plus a 'what it's for' column. Then a client-side duplicate check that flags when two rows share a generic name. That single warning is a genuine safety feature nobody else in the free-printable tier has.

complaints.complaint: Post-discharge is chaos: new prescriptions replace old ones, doses change, some meds are supposed to STOP, and instructions arrive from the hospital, the specialist, the GP and the pharmacy separately. Up to 40% of seniors leave the hospital with incorrect dosages or interacting new prescriptions, and one family member becomes the default coordinator overnight.
complaints.source: NCBI PMC7752204 'Post-discharge medicines management: experiences of older people and family carers'; NCBI PMC10738681 'Inconsistent and Unprepared'; Seniors Blue Book on navigating medication changes after a hospital stay
complaints.weWinIf: Build a first-class 'what changed' state: mark rows NEW / DOSE CHANGED / STOPPED, print stopped meds struck through in a separate DO NOT TAKE block, and stamp the card with a revision date. This is the moment the app is actually opened; design for it explicitly rather than assuming a steady-state list.

complaints.complaint: Caregivers cannot confirm they are holding the right pill. Online identification is unreliable without the imprint code, and generic manufacturers change pill color and shape between refills, so 'the little white oval one' is not an identification.
complaints.source: Drugs.com and WellRx pill identifier guidance ('not possible to accurately identify a pill without an imprint code'); GoodRx guide to creating a medication list, which notes pill colors are a common addition to home med lists
complaints.weWinIf: Give each row a short pill-description field prompting for colour, shape AND imprint code, and print it in words. Do not build a photo feature, photos print as gray smudges on a home printer, which is worse than useless on a fridge card.

tableStakes: Time-of-day grid, Morning / Noon / Evening / Bedtime as columns, medications as rows, with editable clock times (defaults around 8am / 12pm / 6pm / 9pm). Every single competitor template and KeptWell does this; its absence would read as not understanding the category.
Both brand name and generic name on the same row, plus strength (e.g. 'Norvasc / amlodipine 5 mg'). Safety guidance treats this as mandatory, and it is what prevents the classic double-dose error.
A 'what it's for' / indication column. FDA, AHRQ 'My Medicines List' and ASHP 'My Medicine List' all specify it, and it doubles as a sanity check when a dose looks wrong.
Quantity per dose stated as a count, not just a strength, '2 tablets', not '10 mg'. The person at the fridge is counting pills, not doing arithmetic.
An allergies block, visually dominant and impossible to miss, including the reaction ('penicillin, rash, trouble breathing'). Universal on every clinical med-list form.
Prescriber and pharmacy names with phone numbers. Present on the FDA, ASHP, Pitt SilverScripts and VA caregiver med-log templates without exception.
A separate as-needed (PRN) section, physically apart from the scheduled grid, with a max-per-day limit per row. Mixing PRN into the time grid is how people take six of something.
Prints cleanly to exactly one page on both US Letter and A4, with print CSS that does not clip the right column or orphan a row onto page two. A print tool that prints badly has no excuse.

The list persists locally and can be reopened and edited weeks later without retyping, plus a file export/import so it can be moved to another device or handed to a sibling. Doses change constantly; a one-shot generator gets abandoned after the first change.

A live preview of the actual printed page, at true proportions, updating as you type. This is a document generator; if the user has to print to find out what it looks like, the app has failed at its only job.
differentiators: Own the words 'large print' as an actual, measured feature, not a zoom slider. Offer 18 / 22 / 28pt output presets (18pt is the recognized large-print standard per APH, ACB and the Library of Congress NLS; 20pt bold sans-serif is the preferred spec) with a live one-page fit meter that tells you 'fits on one page' or 'drop to 3 meds per card'. Add a 'stand back 3 feet and check' prompt. Nobody in this category quantifies legibility; we can make it the headline.

Print Vial of Life / File of Life compatible. Fold guides for a fridge-magnet pocket, an emergency panel (allergies, conditions, blood type, ICE contacts, advance-directive note), and an optional red header band matching the decal EMS is trained to look for. This plugs a free, EMS-endorsed, county-distributed convention that has no digital front end at all, instant credibility and an obvious pitch to senior centers and fire departments.

Two-up output on one sheet: the big fridge card AND a wallet-size card, with cut lines. The fridge card is for the household; the wallet card is for the ER, the specialist appointment, the pharmacy. Same data, one print job, zero extra work, this is the cheapest high-value feature on the list.

A real no-printer path, because roughly a third of US households have no printer and it skews worse among seniors. Ship: save-as-PDF, the OS share sheet to text/email, and a full-screen 'Fridge Mode', the card at maximum contrast on a propped-up tablet or old phone, screen-wake held on. Plus a one-line tip: most pharmacies, libraries and copy shops will print a PDF you email them.

A 'What changed' revision mode built for discharge day. Tag rows NEW, DOSE CHANGED or STOPPED; stopped meds print struck through in a bordered DO NOT TAKE block; the card carries a revision date and 'replaces card dated ___'. This targets the exact 20 minutes when someone actually opens this app, and no competitor treats the med list as a thing that changes.

A client-side duplicate-ingredient warning. If two rows share a generic name, flag it before printing. Purely local string matching against a small bundled generic/brand list, no backend, no drug database liability, and it addresses the error class behind ~25% of reported medication errors. Frame it carefully as 'double-check with your pharmacist', never as clinical advice.

Bilingual side-by-side printing (English + Spanish to start), for the very common case of a family and a Spanish-speaking home health aide sharing one kitchen. Only the fixed chrome translates, column headers, time-of-day labels, 'as needed', 'do not take', while the user's own med names stay verbatim. Pure client-side string tables, no translation service, no backend.

Lean hard on outliving us. Local file save plus JSON export, plus the optional share-by-link doc so a sibling in another state can open the same card and reprint it, with no accounts on either end. Put the promise in plain words on the page: 'No account. Nothing uploaded. If this site vanishes tomorrow, the card on your fridge still works and your saved file still opens.' After CareZone's shutdown and Medisafe's paywall, that sentence is the whole pitch.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: Today the category is a sea of clinical blue and mint-teal, rounded cards on white, soft gradients, glossy two-tone capsule iconography, and Inter/Roboto/IBM Plex Sans at 14-16px. Medisafe, MyTherapy and the whole App Store long tail are visually interchangeable. What now reads DATED: skeuomorphic pill-bottle and 3D capsule art; hospital-blue gradient headers; pastel mint/lavender 'wellness' palettes; icon-only bottom nav; 12-14px gray-on-white body copy; cutesy mascots (there is a literal 'Cute Pill' app); and confetti/streak gamification, which lands badly when the subject is your mother's heart medication. What reads CURRENT: flat high-contrast surfaces, a generous and obviously deliberate type scale, real words on buttons, and restraint. The bigger opportunity is that everyone in this niche designs a REMINDER APP. We are a document generator. The right visual reference is not Medisafe, it is a good print/label tool: paper preview dead center at true proportions, controls in a calm sidebar, WYSIWYG. Looking like a small print shop rather than a health app is itself the differentiation, and it sets the correct expectation in the first two seconds.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: There are two people here and they are not the same person. THE OPERATOR is an adult child, 45-60, at the kitchen table on hospital-discharge evening, discharge paperwork fanned out, three pharmacy bags, a phone with 40% battery. They are tired, frightened, slightly guilty, and operating on borrowed time before they have to drive home. They will not read instructions, will not create an account, will not watch onboarding. They need to be done in twenty minutes and they need to not make a mistake. Design consequence: no wizard, no modals, no timed anything, autosave every keystroke, everything undoable, forgiving inputs, and no cheerfulness, a friendly 'Great job!' toast here is grating. The secondary operator is the same person six weeks later making a one-line dose change, who must not have to rebuild the card. THE READER is a third party who never touches the app: a 78-year-old with presbyopia and possibly cataracts, standing at the fridge in kitchen light without their reading glasses; or a paid aide who may read English as a second language; or a paramedic at 2am with a flashlight. Design consequence for the OUTPUT: matte black on white, 18pt floor and 22pt default, bold sans-serif, no italics, no all-caps, line spacing at least 1.5, left-aligned blocks, and absolutely no information carried by color alone, home printers are monochrome and a red 'stopped' row prints as gray. Editor UI gets the warmth; the printed card gets near-monochrome discipline. And the tone throughout must be plainspoken and non-alarming: this is a household document, not a medical device, and it should never imply the user is doing something dangerous by using it.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: calm, plainspoken, sturdy, warm, unhurried, dignified

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Warm terracotta / clay, a desaturated earthen orange-red around hue 15-25, e.g. a primary near #B4573C with a deeper #8C3F2A for pressed/active states, sitting on a warm off-white paper ground (#FAF7F3) with near-black warm ink (#221C18) rather than pure #000/#FFF.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Three reasons. First, emotional fit: this artifact lives in a kitchen, not a clinic. Terracotta is the color of a mug, a tile floor, a fired pot, domestic, warm, human, and quietly dignified. It says 'household document' rather than 'medical device', which is exactly the reassurance an exhausted caregiver needs and exactly the framing that keeps us clear of implying clinical authority. Second, category escape: the entire medication space is blue and mint-teal, so a warm earth tone is instantly recognizable as not-another-pill-app and reads as distinct in a 23-app portfolio without resorting to a novelty hue. Third, print discipline: keep the clay strictly in the app chrome and, at most, one hairline header rule and the section labels on the card. The card body stays black-on-white so it survives a monochrome printer and satisfies the large-print contrast standard (bold black on matte white or cream). Critically, RESERVE true red exclusively for the allergies block and the DO NOT TAKE / stopped rows, and pair that red with a heavy border, a rule, and the literal word, never color alone. Because terracotta and warning-red are neighbors, push the brand clay browner and less saturated than you first want, and never place brand clay adjacent to the red safety elements.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Clinical blue (#1E88E5 and family) and mint-teal, the category default, and using it makes us invisible next to Medisafe and MyTherapy. Green as the primary: it is already load-bearing in health UI as 'normal / in range' and it will be misread. Medical-cross red as the identity color, it must stay unspent so it means something on the allergy block. Pastel mint/lavender 'wellness' palettes: low contrast, reads cheap, and fails outright for low-vision users. Any gamified accent system (streak golds, celebration confetti), wrong emotional register entirely for medication. And no color-only encoding anywhere on the printed output: home printers are monochrome, so every colored state needs a redundant word, weight, border or strikethrough.

confidence: MEDIUM-HIGH overall, with specific caveats. HIGH CONFIDENCE and multiply sourced: the Medisafe free-tier collapse (2-med cap Oct 2024, hard paywall Jan 1 2026) and the resulting migration of users, corroborated across four independent competitor blogs plus review-aggregator summaries; the Vial of Life / File of Life fridge convention and EMS familiarity with it (SafeWise, multiple county fire department pages, Island Senior Resources); large-print typographic standards (APH ConnectCenter, American Council of the Blind, Library of Congress NLS all converge on 18pt minimum, 20pt bold sans-serif preferred, 1.5 line spacing, no italics/all-caps, matte black on white); the CareZone/Walmart Wellness retirement on Jan 31 2023 with deactivation of unmigrated accounts; required medication-list fields (FDA, AHRQ, ASHP, VA caregiver log all agree); drug-name confusion as a leading error class (~25%, PA Patient Safety Advisory and PBA Health); post-discharge medication chaos (two peer-reviewed NCBI studies); KeptWell's exact feature set (read directly from the live tool page). WHAT I COULD NOT VERIFY DIRECTLY: Reddit is blocked from this environment, every attempt at reddit.com and old.reddit.com failed, so I have NO first-hand caregiver quotes from r/AgingParents, r/CaregiverSupport or r/dementia. Trustpilot and JustUseApp both returned HTTP 403. That means the user-complaint texture in this report is second-hand, routed through review roundups, competitor comparison blogs, and the TechEnhancedLife older-adult citizen-research panel (which IS a genuine hands-on test of ~20 apps and the best primary-ish source I could reach, though its app-by-app verdicts predate the 2026 Medisafe change). Treat the ad complaints ('unskippable 30-second video after logging a dose') and the 'six taps to schedule a reminder' line as paraphrased aggregations rather than verbatim quotes I read in situ. CONFLICTING DATA: Medisafe's annual price is reported as both $39.99 and $59.88/yr by different sources, confirm before citing a number publicly. DATED FIGURE: the ~62% US household printer-ownership stat is from 2019 and directional only; the no-printer path is justified regardless, but do not publish that number. NOT RESEARCHED, worth a follow-up pass: actual App Store 1-3 star review text for the top 5 apps (needs a non-blocked route), whether any competitor already markets a Vial-of-Life-compatible printable (I found no digital one, but absence of evidence here is weak), and the legal/disclaimer posture other free med-list tools use, worth copying their language before launch.
